scenario: Today's recommendation track has two engineering papers from production systems. Google's Light Heads let YouTube's ranking models take on new targets without retraining, cutting joint experiment time by more than half; Alibaba's RecIS arranges sparse feature processing and dense computation into one pipeline so GPUs wait less. BrowseFlow, from Taobao and Tsinghua, takes a different angle on user simulation: it learns the range of browsing outcomes a user might produce on the same feed instead of copying one log. Several other papers look at side effects of recommendation, including how the feedback loop in location recommendation leaves restaurants empty and makes people of different incomes meet less, and how to remove one user interaction's influence when the model is hosted by someone else.

papers.title: Lightweight Ranking Heads: Accelerating Multi-Task Experimentation in Production Recommender Systems
papers.abstract:
Modern production-scale recommender systems rely on complex, multi-task ranking models. Introducing new prediction tasks into these massive systems often causes bottlenecks - it risks negative task conflicts with existing tasks, and can lead to long development and experimentation cycles due to the expensive retraining of backbone models and downstream models or tuning of reward combination formulas.
To address the critical challenge of slow experimentation velocity, we introduce the Lightweight Ranking Heads (Light Heads) framework. Designed for continuous online learning environments, Light Heads enable the dynamic injection of new tasks into existing multi-task ranking models, effectively obviating the need for model cold-starting and retraining of backbone models.
By utilizing stop-gradients and stateless daily training, this design strictly isolates new tasks, mitigating the risk of adverse task conflicts. Crucially, this framework uses a centralized configuration that allows Light Heads to be added to multiple models simultaneously, unblocking faster training data generation and co-training of downstream models. Successfully deployed at YouTube scale, this approach reduces the iteration cycle for multi-task experimentation from several weeks to days.
In this paper, we detail the system architecture, analyze the training dynamics of stateless cold-started heads, compare their performance to full heads, and demonstrate how Light Heads have enabled the rapid A/B experimentation and deployment of new ranking tasks that yield measurable production value.
papers.authors: Sanjay Surendranath Girija, Aniruddh Nath, Li Wei, Yanhao Jiang, Shawn Andrews, Lukasz Heldt, Yi Wu, Aditya Mahajan, Mohit Sharma
papers.summary: The bigger a multi-task ranking model gets, the slower it becomes to add a new prediction target. YouTube's answer keeps the new target out of the main model and makes it a small prediction head on top of the shared layers (the paper calls it a Light Head). It only reads the shared layers' output, sends no gradient down, and is reset at the start of every training run, and every ranking model reads it from the same config. With the framework, a full experiment cycle covering the ranker and a downstream model shrank from 24 days to 11. The cost is an AUC about 0.01 lower than a fully trained head on data-rich tasks such as clicks.

deep_reading.title: Lightweight Ranking Heads: Accelerating Multi-Task Experimentation in Production Recommender Systems

papers.title: BrowseFlow: Sparse Event Flow Matching for Generative User Simulation
papers.authors: Yitian Pang, Jiayi Zhang, Zhenjia Ma, Xiaowei Yue, Dagui Chen, Jian Xu
papers.abstract: User simulation aims to reproduce how users interact with content and products across online platforms. Recent generative approaches have enriched user simulation with behavioral history and contextual information. However, realistic browsing simulation still faces two challenges. (i) Stochastic Responses: Even with the same recommendation feed, the same user may produce different browsing responses, yielding distinct behavioral trajectories. A logged trajectory records only one such realization. (ii) Sparse Key Events: Clicks and likes provide important feedback but occur sparsely within browsing trajectories dominated by progression actions such as scrolling. Many stepwise simulators predict these actions in a dense sequence, where key events contribute relatively few training targets. To address these challenges, we propose BrowseFlow, a conditional discrete flow matching method for generative user simulation. For Sparse Key Events, BrowseFlow represents each response by its browsing extent and an ordered sequence of key events, directly modeling their counts and locations under exposure constraints. BrowseFlow learns the conditional distribution of complete browsing responses through probabilistic extent prediction and discrete flow matching over key events. Random event retention defines probability paths over partial event sequences, while transition rate matching learns stochastic insertion dynamics. For Stochastic Responses, we use the energy score, a proper scoring rule, to evaluate response fidelity and generated variability, complemented by the Wasserstein distance between key event count distributions. We further introduce TaobaoBrowse, a benchmark pairing real recommendation contexts with fine-grained browsing trajectories. Experiments across three datasets demonstrate that BrowseFlow consistently achieves the best distributional performance.
papers.summary: Shown the same feed, the same user might scroll to item 20 and click two things this time, and leave at item 8 the next; the log keeps only one of these. BrowseFlow argues that a user simulator should learn the distribution of such outcomes rather than copy that one log. It splits a browsing session into two things, how deep the user scrolls and at which positions they click or like, and generates those key events directly instead of predicting a long run of scroll actions step by step. This matters because in Taobao browsing data only 5.48% of actions are positive feedback such as clicks. On three datasets, its generated sessions come closest to real ones both in overall distribution and in click-count distribution.

deep_reading.title: BrowseFlow: Sparse Event Flow Matching for Generative User Simulation

papers.title: Explain, Then Forget: Recommendation Unlearning under Asymmetric Access Constraint
papers.authors: Haichao Zhang, Chong Zhang, Wen Wang, Shi Qiu, Peiyu Hu, Jia Wang
papers.abstract: Recommendation unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific historical interactions that should no longer affect future recommendations, such as noisy clicks or outdated user preferences. However, performing recommendation unlearning becomes much harder in modern Machine-Learning-as-a-Service (MLaaS) architectures, where the recommendation model is remotely hosted by a model provider (MP) and accessed by service operators (SO) only through APIs. In this setting, a service operator serves end users but cannot access or modify internal model parameters. As a result, existing unlearning methods are difficult to apply because they require access to model internals for retraining, fine-tuning, or other parameter updates. To address these challenges, we propose Causal Explanation-based Unlearning (CEU), a novel unlearning framework tailored for MLaaS environments. Instead of modifying internal model weights, CEU operates through a two-step output-level score intervention. First, it estimates how the forgotten interaction causally contributes to the current recommendation. Second, guided by this causal signal, the system removes the influence of the forgotten interaction by adjusting the final ranking scores of affected items. Because CEU leaves model parameters untouched, it naturally supports continuous unlearning requests while avoiding the error accumulation that can result from repeated parameter updates. Extensive experiments on three public datasets show that CEU achieves unlearning effectiveness comparable to full retraining while preserving recommendation utility and significantly reducing computational cost. The source code is available at: https://github.com/zhang-haichao/Explain-and-Forget.
papers.summary: In many apps the recommendation model is hosted by an outside provider, and the operator can only call an API for scores without touching the model's parameters. When a user then asks to remove a mis-click or an outdated interaction, existing recommendation unlearning methods do not apply, because they retrain or fine-tune the model. CEU leaves the model alone and changes only its output. The model provider precomputes how much each past interaction contributes to each recommendation, that is, how much the item's score would drop without that interaction, and serves it through the API. On a removal request, the operator subtracts that contribution from the affected items' scores and re-ranks. On three public datasets it forgets about as well as full retraining. One removal request takes at most 6.37 seconds, while full retraining takes from minutes to over an hour.

papers.title: Fair Recommender Systems for Intersecting Groups
papers.abstract: Recommendation systems that optimize for the average user can fail to capture the preferences of diverse demographic groups. We consider a dynamic recommendation system, where arriving users can belong to different demographic groups. Importantly, these groups can intersect, and a user may belong to several groups. We first show that over time, any group-blind policy (which excludes all current-user group information) recommending $K \geq 1$ items incurs linear total regret under mild conditions. In turn, we introduce three group-aware algorithms based on the classical Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB): i) Intersection-Fitting, which runs UCB on each intersection, but has a sublinear group- and intersection-level regret guarantee with an exponential dependence in the number of groups; and ii) two group-level heuristics, Inner-Outer UCB and Group-Item UCB which allocate different arms to different groups, and use a sleeping expert meta-learner to choose which active group's recommendation an intersection should inherit at any given time step. We provide experimental results on two datasets, Goodreads and BoardGameGeek, and highlight that our heuristics can be preferable to the intersection-fitting algorithm when intersection-level preferences are closely related to group-level preferences, but that intersection-fitting performs better when different intersections within a same group prefer different items.
papers.summary: If a recommender ignores which group a user belongs to and serves the average taste of all users, minority groups keep losing out. The authors prove that whenever the overall favourite set of items is not the best one for some group, this policy's cumulative gap to each group's best recommendations grows linearly with time. The hard part is that groups overlap, so one person can belong to several at once. The authors offer two routes. One learns preferences separately for every combination of groups, which has a guarantee but leaves each combination with little data once there are many. The other learns per broad group first, and a selector uses past feedback to decide which of its groups' recommendations each combination follows at the moment. On two datasets, the second route wins when combinations share their broad groups' taste, and the first wins when they differ.

papers.title: Recommendation Feedback Loops Shape Urban Income Segregation and Venue Visitation
papers.authors: Guangyuan Weng, Lin Chen, Ciro Beneduce, Giovanni Mauro, Massimiliano Luca, Takahiro Yabe, Bruno Lepri, Luca Pappalardo, Esteban Moro
papers.abstract: Location-based recommender systems shape where people go in cities and learn from the visits they steer, forming a human-AI feedback loop. This feedback loop shapes whom people share places with across income groups and which venues keep attracting customers. Yet platforms judge these systems by their offline accuracy on past visits, a test in which the suggestions never change where people go and which therefore cannot capture long-term effects. Studying these effects in cities is challenging because, unlike online resources, travel constraints and limited venue capacity shape where people can go, while each recommended visit also changes whom other visitors encounter. To capture such features, we build a long-term simulation framework based on fine-grained human mobility data from four U.S. metropolitan areas, with distance and capacity constraints. Focusing on food venues, we study two urban consequences: how unevenly people's exposure is distributed across income groups (experienced income segregation) and the share of venues receiving no visits from simulated residents (venue disappearance). We find that, under every algorithm and in every metropolitan area, at least a fifth of venues stop receiving visits, and that more than half of this loss arises from retraining. More importantly, more accurate algorithms leave people more segregated, and the most accurate algorithm leaves people 15-21% more segregated than they actually are. We then test a re-ranking intervention that favours less popular venues and runs on top of a platform's existing algorithm. It lowers both venue disappearance and segregation across algorithms, largely without directing people to venues where they may feel less comfortable. Our results suggest that impact assessments of recommender systems should account for the feedback loop and report segregation and venue disappearance beyond accuracy.
papers.summary: Location recommendations change where people go to eat, and the platform retrains on the visits it steered, closing a loop. Offline accuracy cannot measure this loop's long-term effect, so the authors ran long-term simulations on real mobility data from four US metro areas, accounting for travel distance and venue capacity. Under every algorithm and in every city, at least a fifth of food venues end up with no visitors, and more than half of that loss comes from repeated retraining. The paper measures this as income segregation: the more the people someone meets at venues lean toward one income band, the higher it is. More accurate algorithms give higher segregation, and the most accurate is 15% to 21% above residents' real visits. Re-ranking on top of the existing recommender to favour less popular venues eases both problems.

papers.title: RecIS: Unifying Sparse and Dense Computation for Efficient Recommendation Training
papers.authors: Hua Zong, Shuai Yang, Zhengxiong Zhou, Qingtao Zeng, Jiawei Liu, Hao Wan, Hongbin Zhou, Jiahao Wang, Hao Zhang, Bencheng Yan, Yuheng Huang, Huimin Yi, Jiamang Wang, Han Zhu, Jian Xu, Bo Zheng, Lin Qu
papers.abstract: Modern recommender models scale sparse representations and dense computation together. They process thousands of heterogeneous feature fields, long user-behavior sequences, and trillion-scale Embedding parameters, while their dense networks increasingly use large Transformer architectures. The resulting execution mismatch creates fine-grained operations within stages, load imbalance and synchronization delays across devices, and GPU resource bubbles between stages. As models grow, these costs become a primary limit to scalable recommender training. Although existing systems improve Embedding caching and data prefetching, these inefficiencies still coexist in the GPU-centric workloads we study and jointly limit end-to-end throughput. We present RecIS, a unified framework for GPU-centric recommender training. RecIS treats the complete path from input features to dense computation as one optimization target and coordinates three complementary mechanisms. First, adaptive fusion combines fragmented feature transformations with vectorized memory access. Second, a GPU Embedding engine uses hash-based sharding and hierarchical communication to balance request placement and eliminate redundant transfers; it also specializes aggregation for forward and backward index structures. Third, a multistage pipeline overlaps input preparation for future iterations with dense computation in the current iteration. Together, these mechanisms reorganize a fragmented sparse front end into a dataflow that continuously feeds dense computation. We evaluate RecIS on representative industrial recommender models across distributed training platforms. Compared with PICASSO and TorchRec, RecIS reaches up to $2.62\times$ and $1.15\times$ their throughput, respectively, while reducing step latency by up to 61.5\% and 12.9\%. RecIS provides an efficient and scalable training system for large recommender models.
papers.summary: In recommender training, the first half handles thousands of feature fields and trillion-scale embedding tables with small, random operations, while the second half is an ever larger Transformer doing dense, regular computation. With both on the same GPUs, the GPUs often sit waiting for data. Alibaba's RecIS optimizes the whole path from raw features to dense computation as one unit. It merges scattered feature transforms into larger operators and spreads embedding lookups evenly across GPUs by hashing, removing duplicate transfers. It also prepares the inputs for upcoming steps while the current step runs its dense computation. On industrial recommender models, throughput reaches up to 1.15 times that of TorchRec and 2.62 times that of PICASSO.

papers.title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
papers.authors: Yin Yi, Haiping Ma, Siyu Song, Ziwen Wang, Shangshang Yang
papers.abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.
papers.summary: A newly launched question platform has question texts but no answer logs to train on yet. Can a model trained on other platforms predict whether a student will get the next question right? Carrying question-text semantics over as features works poorly, because question styles differ a lot across platforms. TIZSKT uses text only as an index for finding similar questions. The model itself learns only how right and wrong answers evolve, without question IDs or text. At prediction time, the questions this student just answered on the new platform, and whether they got them right, are known. The model uses the text to pick those resembling the current question, summarizes how the student did on them, and combines that with its learned answering state to compute the chance of a correct answer. The new platform needs no training, and on three public datasets it has the highest mean AUC.

papers.title: Towards Trustworthy Multi-stakeholder Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Katarina Marcincinova, Adrian Gavornik, Matus Mesarcik, Michal Kompan
papers.abstract: Recommender system (RS) nowadays has to reflect, combine, and solve often contrasting requirements and expectations from dozens of stakeholders. In fact, the problem is even more complicated as each of the stakeholders can simultaneously have various objectives creating a diverse and complicated environment with several stakeholders and their objectives in which a RS operates. To address this problems the Multi-objective and Multi-stakeholder RS have been studied in the literature. However, a limited attention has been paid to trustworthiness aspects of such RS, which slowly becomes a new standard. In this paper, we highlight open challenges and important questions which need to be addressed on the way to trustworthy Multi-stakeholder RS.
papers.summary: A recommender has to serve users, content creators and the platform, plus developers, regulators and society at large, and each party has several goals. Multi-stakeholder, multi-objective recommendation has been studied a fair amount, but few ask whether such systems can be trusted. This position paper argues that trust is not only about fewer biases and privacy problems; it also means actively respecting human values and handling conflicts between parties' goals. Its example: a creator promoting healthy-diet videos is harmless in itself, but pushing them to a user with an eating disorder can do harm. The paper has no new method or experiments and lists four open problems: whom to treat fairly under multiple objectives, how to turn human values into measurable goals, the computing cost of more objectives, and EU rules requiring platforms to explain what drives their recommendations.
